cards.q: What are the three core problems Git exists to solve?
cards.a: Losing working versions, being unable to work on two things at once, and being unable to mechanically combine two people's edits.

cards.q: Why does manual folder-copying (project-v2-final) fail as a version control strategy?
cards.a: It gives you no record of what changed between copies, no explanation of why, no ordering guarantee, and duplicates the entire folder's storage every time.

cards.q: Why can't two people just each edit their own copy of a project folder?
cards.a: There's no mechanical way to combine the two folders afterward — someone has to manually compare every file and decide, line by line, which edits to keep.

cards.q: What does Git actually store when you make a commit — the changes, or something else?
cards.a: A complete snapshot of every file's state at that instant, not a diff.

cards.q: If Git stores full snapshots every time, why doesn't a repository's size explode?
cards.a: Files are named by a hash of their content. If a file's contents are unchanged since the last snapshot, hashing it produces the same name, and it's already in storage — nothing new gets written.

cards.q: What is a blob?
cards.a: The raw contents of one file — nothing else. No filename, no path, no permissions.

cards.q: If a blob has no filename, where does the filename live?
cards.a: In a tree — the object type that lists directory entries (name, mode, and the hash of the blob or tree it refers to).

cards.q: What is a tree, precisely?
cards.a: A directory listing: a sorted set of entries, each mapping a name to a blob (file) or another tree (subdirectory).

cards.q: What is a commit object, and what does it point to?
cards.a: A record of one snapshot: it points to exactly one tree (the project's root directory at that instant), plus author, committer, timestamp, and message.

cards.q: Why does renaming a file not create a new blob?
cards.a: The file's contents didn't change, only its name — and the name lives in the tree, not the blob. Renaming creates a new tree entry that still points at the same blob.

cards.q: Why can Git not represent an empty directory?
cards.a: A tree only contains entries; there's nothing to list for an empty directory, so no tree object can represent it. This is why .gitkeep exists as a convention.

cards.q: What two properties does content-addressing (naming objects by hash) give you for free?
cards.a: Deduplication — identical content is only ever stored once — and integrity — if content is altered, its hash no longer matches its name, so tampering is detectable.

cards.q: What command initializes the object store?
cards.a: git init.

cards.q: What single field turns a pile of unordered snapshots into a history?
cards.a: The parent field on a commit — each commit records the identifier of the commit before it.

cards.q: What is a root commit?
cards.a: A commit with no parent — the first commit in a repository's history.

cards.q: Why is Git's history described as 'tamper-evident'? What's the actual mechanism?
cards.a: A commit's identifier is a hash of its content, which includes its parent's identifier. Change anything anywhere in the history and every identifier after that point changes, because each one transitively depends on everything before it.

cards.q: What does git log actually do, mechanically?
cards.a: Starts at the current commit and walks parent pointers backward, printing each commit it visits.

cards.q: What's the difference between what git log shows you and what git show <commit> shows you?
cards.a: git log walks and lists a range of commits; git show inspects the full content of one specific object.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: Why can't a commit simply record 'everything currently in the folder'?
cards.a: A working folder is never all one thing — it's a mix of finished work, half-finished work, and junk. All-or-nothing snapshotting can't separate them.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What is the index (staging area), physically?
cards.a: A real file, .git/index, listing paths and the identifier of the blob that will be recorded for each at the next commit.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: Name the three states of a Git project and what each represents.
cards.a: Working tree (files on disk), index (what the next commit will contain), HEAD (what the last commit did contain).

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What does git add actually do?
cards.a: Hashes the file's current contents, writes it as a blob into the object store, and points the index at that blob for that path.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What does git commit do, in terms of the index?
cards.a: Converts the index into a tree (and subtrees), then writes a commit object pointing at the resulting root tree.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: git status reports staged changes, unstaged changes, and untracked files. What comparisons produce each?
cards.a: Staged = index vs HEAD. Unstaged = working tree vs index. Untracked = files on disk the index has never recorded.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What are the three forms of git diff, and what does each compare?
cards.a: git diff = working tree vs index. git diff --staged = index vs HEAD. git diff HEAD = working tree vs HEAD.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What does git add -p let you do that plain git add doesn't?
cards.a: Stage individual hunks within a file rather than the whole file, making it possible to split one file's changes into separate logical commits.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: Why is git commit -a considered a bad habit?
cards.a: It stages all tracked modifications automatically, bypassing deliberate use of the index and encouraging non-atomic, tangled commits.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: Why is git status fast even on a large project with thousands of files?
cards.a: The index caches each file's size and modification time from when it was last hashed. Only files whose stat data changed get re-hashed.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What does adding a pattern to .gitignore do to a file Git is already tracking?
cards.a: Nothing. Ignore rules only apply to untracked files.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: If a tracked file needs to become ignored, what's the actual fix?
cards.a: Remove it from tracking with git rm --cached, then let .gitignore take effect going forward.

cards.t: Node 3 · The index and the three trees
cards.q: What's the difference between .gitignore, .git/info/exclude, and the global ignore file?
cards.a: gitignore is shared and committed; .git/info/exclude is local to your clone and not shared; the global ignore file applies across all your repositories, typically for OS/editor junk.

cards.q: What is a ref, physically?
cards.a: A file, typically under .git/refs/, whose entire contents is a commit identifier.

cards.q: What is a branch, precisely?
cards.a: A ref — a movable pointer to a commit. refs/heads/main is a small text file containing a hash.

cards.q: Why is creating a Git branch cheap, unlike an SVN-style branch?
cards.a: It costs writing one small file containing a hash — no copying of files or history is involved.

cards.q: What happens to a branch's ref file when you commit while on that branch?
cards.a: Git writes the new commit, then overwrites the branch's ref file with the new commit's identifier — the branch pointer follows you forward.

cards.q: What is HEAD, and what does it normally contain?
cards.a: A file that tracks your current position; normally it contains a symbolic reference like ref: refs/heads/main — a pointer to a branch, which is itself a pointer to a commit.

cards.q: Does a commit know what branch it's on?
cards.a: No. Branch membership isn't stored anywhere — 'commits on a branch' means commits reachable by walking parent pointers starting from that branch's pointer.

cards.q: Why can one commit be reachable from multiple branches?
cards.a: Because branch membership is reachability, not an attribute stored on the commit — any branch whose pointer can reach that commit through parent links 'contains' it.

cards.q: What happens to a commit when its branch is deleted?
cards.a: Nothing happens to the commit itself — only the pointer (the ref file) is deleted. The commit remains in the object store, unreferenced.

cards.q: What is detached HEAD?
cards.a: A state where HEAD points directly at a commit identifier instead of at a branch — a position with no branch attached.

cards.q: Is detached HEAD an error state?
cards.a: No — it's normal, and Git puts you there deliberately during operations like checking out a specific commit or during a bisect step.

cards.q: Why are new commits made in detached HEAD at risk of being lost?
cards.a: Nothing points at them — no branch follows along — so once you switch away, they become unreferenced and unreachable except via the reflog until it expires.

cards.q: What's the difference between git switch and the older git checkout?
cards.a: git checkout was overloaded to handle branch switching, file restoration, and detached HEAD all at once; git switch isolates just the branch-switching job.

cards.q: What does HEAD~3 mean?
cards.a: Walk back three commits along first-parent ancestry from HEAD.

cards.q: What does HEAD^2 mean, and when does it apply?
cards.a: The second parent of the current commit — only meaningful on a merge commit, which has more than one parent.

cards.q: What does main@{1} mean?
cards.a: Where the main ref pointed one move ago, according to the reflog.

cards.q: What does the range main..feature mean?
cards.a: Commits reachable from feature but not from main — i.e., 'what's on my branch that main doesn't have.'

cards.q: How does main...feature (three dots) differ from main..feature?
cards.a: It's the symmetric difference — commits reachable from either branch but not both, rather than one-directional.

cards.q: What's the difference between a lightweight tag and an annotated tag?
cards.a: A lightweight tag is just a ref pointing directly at a commit. An annotated tag is a real object with its own hash, carrying a tagger, date, message, and optional signature.

cards.q: Are tags pushed to a remote by default?
cards.a: No — tags require an explicit git push --tags (or --follow-tags).

cards.q: Before Git can combine two branches, what does it need to compute first?
cards.a: The merge base — the most recent commit reachable from both branches.

cards.q: What is a fast-forward merge, and why does it create no new commit?
cards.a: It happens when the merge base equals your current commit — meaning your branch hasn't moved since diverging. Git just slides your branch pointer forward to the other branch's tip; nothing needs combining.

cards.q: What is a three-way merge?
cards.a: A comparison of base-vs-ours and base-vs-theirs for each file: if only one side changed a region, take that side's version; if both changed it identically, take it once; if both changed it differently, it's a conflict.

cards.q: What actually causes a merge conflict?
cards.a: Both branches changed the same region of the same file differently since their common ancestor, so Git has no rule to decide which version to keep.

cards.q: Does a conflict mean someone made a mistake?
cards.a: No — it means two people edited overlapping lines since the merge base. It's a normal consequence of parallel work.

cards.q: What do the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers represent?
cards.a: <<<<<<< through ======= is your version (ours); ======= through >>>>>>> is the incoming version (theirs).

cards.q: What does setting merge.conflictStyle to zdiff3 add to a conflict?
cards.a: It also shows the common ancestor's version of the region (marked with |||||||), which often makes it obvious what each side actually changed.

cards.q: What is a merge commit, structurally?
cards.a: A commit with two parents, recording that two divergent lines of history were combined into one.

cards.q: Why does real Git history usually look like a graph rather than a straight line?
cards.a: Merge commits have two parents, and repeated branching and merging produces a directed acyclic graph, not a chain.

cards.q: What does --no-ff do, and why would you use it?
cards.a: Forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving the historical fact that a separate branch existed.

cards.q: What does a squash merge do, and why does the source branch still show as 'unmerged' afterward?
cards.a: It applies all the branch's changes as one new commit with no merge link back to the original commits — so by ancestry, none of the original branch's commits are actually reachable from main.

cards.q: What is --abort for, during a merge?
cards.a: It cancels the in-progress merge and returns you to the state before you started — the same escape hatch pattern used by rebase, cherry-pick, and revert.

cards.q: What is a semantic conflict, and why is it more dangerous than a textual one?
cards.a: A merge that succeeds with no marked conflict, but breaks the build — e.g., one side renamed a function the other side still calls. Git's merge algorithm only compares text, not meaning.

cards.q: Why does CI typically run against the merge result rather than against each branch individually?
cards.a: Because semantic conflicts are invisible to Git's merge algorithm and only surface when the combined code actually runs or builds.

cards.q: What foundational fact makes history rewriting safe?
cards.a: Objects are immutable — rewriting never edits an existing object, it only creates new objects and moves pointers. Originals remain in the store.

cards.q: What does git commit --amend actually do?
cards.a: Creates a new commit object replacing the most recent one, with a new identifier — it does not edit the original commit.

cards.q: What does git cherry-pick do?
cards.a: Applies the change introduced by one commit onto your current position, as a new commit — internally a three-way merge where the base is the picked commit's parent.

cards.q: What is git rebase, mechanically?
cards.a: Take every commit unique to your branch, replay each one's change onto a different base commit in order, then move the branch pointer to the end of the replayed sequence.

cards.q: Why do commits produced by a rebase have different identifiers than the originals?
cards.a: They're new objects — same diff, but a different parent and therefore a different hash, since a commit's identifier depends on its parent's identifier.

cards.q: In interactive rebase, what does squash do versus fixup?
cards.a: Both fold a commit into the one before it; squash keeps and lets you edit the combined commit message, fixup discards the folded commit's message entirely.

cards.q: What does git commit --fixup combined with rebase --autosquash accomplish?
cards.a: Lets you mark a correction as belonging to an earlier commit as you make it, then automatically places and folds it into that commit during the next rebase.

cards.q: What is --onto used for?
cards.a: Transplanting a range of commits onto an arbitrary different base — the fix for 'I branched off the wrong branch.'

cards.q: What's the real trade-off between merge and rebase?
cards.a: Merge preserves what actually happened, including parallel lines of work, at the cost of a harder-to-read history. Rebase produces a clean linear history at the cost of misrepresenting the actual sequence of events and changing commit identifiers.

cards.q: Why is it dangerous to rebase a branch other people have already pulled?
cards.a: Their copy still references the old commit identifiers; after your rebase, those commits no longer exist on your side, so their history diverges from yours in a way that's painful to reconcile.

cards.q: Why is it possible to recover from most Git mistakes?
cards.a: Nothing is ever truly deleted — operations only make commits unreferenced (nothing points at them), and unreferenced objects persist until garbage collection eventually removes them.

cards.q: What does git reset --soft do?
cards.a: Moves HEAD (and the branch it points to) to a different commit. Index and working tree are untouched — your changes remain staged.

cards.q: What does git reset --mixed (the default) do?
cards.a: Moves HEAD and resets the index to match the new HEAD. Changes remain on disk but become unstaged.

cards.q: What does git reset --hard do?
cards.a: Moves HEAD, resets the index, and overwrites the working tree to match — any uncommitted changes are discarded.

cards.q: What's the difference between git restore --staged and git restore --worktree?
cards.a: --staged unstages a file (moves it out of the index back toward HEAD's version), --worktree discards working-tree changes and reverts the file to the index's version.

cards.q: How does git revert differ from git reset in what it does to history?
cards.a: revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an old one — history gains an entry. reset moves a pointer backward, potentially making commits unreferenced.

cards.q: Why is git revert the correct tool for undoing a commit that's already been pushed and shared?
cards.a: It adds a new commit rather than rewriting or removing anything, so nobody else's history becomes invalid or diverges.

cards.q: What does git stash do, and what is a stash internally?
cards.a: Shelves uncommitted working-tree and index changes so you can switch context cleanly. A stash is stored as an ordinary commit under a hidden ref.

cards.q: What is the reflog?
cards.a: A local, per-repository log that records every value HEAD and each branch has held, appended to every time one of them changes.

cards.q: How do you use the reflog to recover from a bad reset --hard?
cards.a: Run git reflog to find the commit identifier from before the reset, then git reset --hard <that-identifier> to return to it.

cards.q: Does the reflog persist forever?
cards.a: No — reachable entries expire (default roughly 90 days) and unreachable ones expire faster (default roughly 30 days); after expiry and garbage collection, recovery via reflog is no longer possible.

cards.q: Why must you always run git clean with -n first?
cards.a: git clean deletes untracked files, which were never in the object store at any point — there is no recovery mechanism for them. -n previews what would be deleted without deleting it.

cards.q: What is ORIG_HEAD, and when does Git set it?
cards.a: A scratch ref Git writes before dangerous operations (like reset or a merge), recording where HEAD was beforehand — a quick manual undo target.

cards.q: What is a remote, precisely?
cards.a: A name mapped to a URL — origin is just a convention, not a keyword. You can have any number of remotes.

cards.q: What does it mean that 'every clone is a complete repository'?
cards.a: Each clone holds the full object store and full history independently — there's no partial copy, and no central authority built into Git itself. Any clone could act as the source of truth.

cards.q: What does git fetch actually do?
cards.a: Downloads objects the remote has that you don't, and updates your remote-tracking branches. It does not touch your working tree, your index, or your local branches.

cards.q: What is a remote-tracking branch like origin/main, and is it live?
cards.a: A local ref recording where the remote's main stood at your last fetch. It is not live — it can be stale until you fetch again.

cards.q: What does git pull do that git fetch doesn't?
cards.a: It fetches, then performs an integration step — merging by default, or rebasing if pull.rebase is configured.

cards.q: Why do repositories often accumulate accidental 'Merge branch main of...' commits?
cards.a: Because git pull's default integration step is a merge, and people run pull without realizing an implicit merge is happening.

cards.q: What does git push do, and when does the remote refuse it?
cards.a: Uploads your objects and asks the remote to move one of its refs to your new commit. It's refused if the move wouldn't be a fast-forward — i.e., if it would make commits the remote currently has unreachable.

cards.q: Why does pushing a rebased branch typically get rejected?
cards.a: The rebase produced new commit identifiers with a different history shape, so your branch no longer descends from what the remote has — the push isn't a fast-forward.

cards.q: What does --force-with-lease do differently from plain --force?
cards.a: It refuses to push if the remote has moved since your last fetch, protecting against overwriting someone else's work — the actual risk force-pushing poses — while still allowing you to overwrite your own unshared history.

cards.q: What does upstream tracking configuration actually do?
cards.a: Lets bare git push and git pull know which remote and branch to talk to, without you specifying them each time — set via -u on the first push.

cards.q: What is a refspec?
cards.a: The mapping that defines what a fetch or push actually moves — e.g., +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/* maps every remote branch to a local remote-tracking branch.

cards.q: What does git fetch --prune do?
cards.a: Deletes local remote-tracking branches whose corresponding branch no longer exists on the remote.

cards.q: What is a bare repository?
cards.a: A repository with no working tree — just the .git contents at the root. This is what every server-side repository actually is.

cards.q: What does a shallow clone (--depth) trade away?
cards.a: Full history, in exchange for downloading only recent commits — commonly used in CI where full history isn't needed.

cards.q: Why is embedding a token directly in an HTTPS remote URL a security risk?
cards.a: The token ends up stored in plaintext in .git/config and often in shell history, both of which can leak.

cards.q: Are pull requests a Git feature or a platform feature?
cards.a: A platform feature (e.g., GitHub) — Git itself has no concept of a pull request.

cards.q: What is trunk-based development?
cards.a: Everyone integrates into main frequently via short-lived branches, rather than maintaining long-lived parallel branches.

cards.q: What is the feature-branch-plus-pull-request workflow?
cards.a: Branch off, push, open a pull request, get it reviewed, then merge — the standard collaborative pattern on GitHub-style platforms.

cards.q: What is Git Flow, and why has it fallen out of favor?
cards.a: A heavyweight model with permanent develop, release/*, and hotfix/* branches. It's largely been abandoned in favor of trunk-based development because continuous delivery doesn't need or want long-lived parallel branches.

cards.q: What distinguishes fork-and-PR from a standard feature branch workflow?
cards.a: In fork-and-PR you push to your own copy of the repository (since you can't write to the original) and request that your changes be pulled into a repository you don't have write access to — the standard open-source contribution model.

cards.q: What does a regular merge button do to history, versus squash, versus rebase-merge?
cards.a: Merge: keeps all the branch's individual commits and adds a two-parent merge commit. Squash: collapses everything into one new commit with no merge link. Rebase-merge: replays the commits onto the tip with new identifiers and no merge commit at all.

cards.q: Why do smaller, shorter-lived pull requests reduce conflict risk?
cards.a: The longer a branch lives, the further its merge base recedes from the current tip of main, increasing the amount of divergence and therefore the chance of overlapping changes.

cards.q: What is CODEOWNERS, and is it a Git concept?
cards.a: A platform-level (not Git) file specifying who must review changes to specific paths — enforced by the hosting platform, not by Git itself.

cards.q: What are hooks?
cards.a: Scripts Git runs automatically at defined points — e.g., pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push locally, or pre-receive on the server.

cards.q: Why don't hooks travel with a clone by default?
cards.a: .git/hooks is not part of the tracked repository content — it lives outside version control, so a fresh clone starts with no hooks at all.

cards.q: What problem does core.hooksPath solve?
cards.a: It points Git at a tracked, shareable directory for hooks instead of the untracked .git/hooks, so hooks can be committed and distributed with the repo.

cards.q: What does --no-verify reveal about the nature of hooks?
cards.a: That hooks are a convenience, not a security control — anyone can trivially bypass them.

cards.q: What is the Conventional Commits format?
cards.a: A structured commit message prefix like feat:, fix:, or chore: with an optional scope, designed to be machine-parseable.

cards.q: What does Conventional Commits formatting enable that free-text messages don't?
cards.a: Automated changelog generation and automatic semantic version bumping, since tooling can parse the type of each change.

cards.q: Why does CI running on the merge result (rather than either branch alone) matter?
cards.a: It's the only way to catch semantic conflicts — changes that don't textually conflict but break when combined.

cards.q: Why does commit signing matter, given that author/committer fields are just plain text?
cards.a: Anyone can set user.email to someone else's address, making the author field an unverified claim. Signing (increasingly via SSH keys) makes authorship cryptographically verifiable.

cards.q: What does a secret-scanning pre-commit hook actually prevent?
cards.a: It stops a credential from ever entering history in the first place — far cheaper than the cleanup required once something is committed and pushed.

cards.q: What's the difference between git log --stat and git log -p?
cards.a: --stat shows which files changed and how many lines, as a summary. -p shows the actual diff content for each commit.

cards.q: What does git log -S 'someString' (the pickaxe) find?
cards.a: Commits where the number of occurrences of that exact string changed — added or removed — which is the fastest way to find when a specific piece of code was introduced or deleted.

cards.q: How does git log -G differ from git log -S?
cards.a: -G matches commits where a regex pattern's presence changed in the diff at all (even if the occurrence count stayed the same, e.g. a line moved); -S strictly tracks a change in occurrence count.

cards.q: What does git blame show you, per line?
cards.a: The commit (and author) that last modified each line of a file.

cards.q: Why would you pass -w to git blame?
cards.a: To ignore whitespace-only changes, so a line's 'true' last meaningful change is attributed correctly instead of to a reformatting commit.

cards.q: What do -M and -C do for git blame?
cards.a: Let it detect lines that were moved (-M) or copied (-C) within or between files, rather than attributing them to whoever's commit happened to reintroduce them.

cards.q: What is .git-blame-ignore-revs for?
cards.a: A file listing commit hashes (typically large reformatting or auto-fix commits) that git blame should skip over, attributing lines to the change before them instead.

cards.q: What is git bisect, mechanically?
cards.a: A binary search over commit history: you mark one known-good and one known-bad commit, and Git checks out the midpoint repeatedly, halving the search range each time until it isolates the exact commit that introduced the bug.

cards.q: What does git bisect run <script> do?
cards.a: Fully automates the bisect process by running the given script at each checked-out commit and using its exit code to decide good or bad, without manual intervention.

cards.q: Why does git bisect depend on commits being atomic and individually buildable?
cards.a: Because it checks out arbitrary intermediate commits and tests them in isolation — if a commit represents a half-finished, non-building state, bisect can't meaningfully evaluate it.

cards.q: How does git grep differ from a plain recursive grep -r?
cards.a: It searches Git's tracked content directly (and can search at any historical revision), and is significantly faster since it operates on Git's internal data rather than walking the filesystem.

cards.q: What problem does git range-diff solve?
cards.a: It compares two versions of a rewritten branch (e.g., before and after a rebase), letting you review what actually changed in the rebase rather than re-reading the entire diff from scratch.

cards.q: What is a packfile?
cards.a: A file that consolidates many individual objects into one, storing similar objects as deltas (differences) against each other for compression — this is the actual source of Git's storage efficiency.

cards.q: Is a packfile a contradiction of 'Git stores full snapshots'?
cards.a: No — it's a storage optimization layer beneath the snapshot model. Conceptually every commit still points to a full tree; packfiles are just how that content gets compressed on disk.

cards.q: What does git gc do?
cards.a: Packs loose objects into packfiles, packs refs, and prunes unreferenced objects that are older than the expiry window.

cards.q: What's the relationship between git gc and the reflog-based recovery from Node 7?
cards.a: git gc is the operation that actually removes unreferenced objects once their expiry window passes — it's what turns 'recoverable but unreferenced' into genuinely gone.

cards.q: Why doesn't deleting a large committed binary in a later commit shrink the repository?
cards.a: The old snapshot still references the old blob in history — deleting the file only changes what future snapshots contain, not what past ones did. Only rewriting history removes the blob from storage.

cards.q: What problem does Git LFS solve?
cards.a: It stores large binary files outside the main repository, leaving small pointer files inside it — avoiding the size and performance problems of large binaries in Git's own object store.

cards.q: What is a submodule?
cards.a: A pin inside your repository referencing another repository at an exact commit.

cards.q: Why does checking out a submodule often leave it in detached HEAD?
cards.a: A submodule is pinned to a specific commit, not a branch — so Git checks out that exact commit, which by definition has no branch pointer attached.

cards.q: What is a Git worktree, and what problem does it solve better than stashing?
cards.a: A second working directory checked out from a different branch, sharing the same underlying object store. It lets you work on two branches simultaneously without shelving and restoring state via stash.

cards.q: Once a secret is committed and pushed, what is the correct first action?
cards.a: Rotate the credential immediately — treat it as compromised regardless of whether anyone is known to have seen it.

cards.q: Why is git filter-repo preferred over the older git filter-branch?
cards.a: filter-branch is deprecated and extremely slow on large histories; filter-repo is the modern, faster, safer tool for rewriting history at scale.

cards.q: After purging a secret from history with filter-repo and force-pushing, is the secret actually gone?
cards.a: Not necessarily everywhere — any existing clones or forks made before the purge still contain the old objects with the secret. Rewriting cleans the canonical repository but can't reach copies already made.

cards.q: Why is exposing a .git directory on a public web server dangerous?
cards.a: It exposes the entire object store and history — anyone can reconstruct the full source code and every past version, including anything since removed.

cards.q: What is a signed tag, and why would you use one?
cards.a: An annotated tag with a cryptographic signature attached, giving release integrity — verifying that a specific release point genuinely came from a trusted author, the same idea as commit signing applied to releases.
